title: Assessing Communicative Performance

pts: A rubric that scores only grammatical accuracy has a validity problem in Unit 21's sense — it doesn't measure communicative competence, only one component of it.
This quietly teaches learners that only grammar matters, undermining the sociolinguistic and discourse work this tier builds.
Rubric design is where a course's stated aims either become real or remain aspirational.

v: Two or three rubrics or marking schemes currently in use

items: Collect the rubrics or marking schemes you use for speaking and writing, including the board’s.
Label each criterion: grammatical, sociolinguistic, discourse or strategic.
Count the marks attached to each component.
Compare the result with the aims stated for the task in your scheme of work (Unit 14).
Identify one mismatch and draft a replacement criterion.
In a teacher circle, audit the school’s common examination marking scheme together.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: An audit of a typical ‘letter to the editor’ marking scheme (written for this book):

lines: Grammar and spelling: 6 marks → grammatical.
Format (address, date, subject line): 2 marks → partly discourse (genre).
Content: 2 marks → unclear; not linked to any competence.
Nothing rewards tone, argument structure or awareness of the reader.

blocks.x: The scheme claims to assess letter writing, but 60 per cent of its marks measure sentence-level accuracy.

body: Purpose: to show the narrowness of a grammar-only rubric. Content: a speech bubble with four labelled strands (grammar, appropriacy, organization, repair); a magnifying glass labelled ‘rubric’ picks up only the grammar strand. Style: clean diagram, labels as well as colours. Board version: a circle divided into four with only one quarter shaded.

items: Google Sheets (free) to tabulate marks by component across several rubrics.

blocks.x: A four-column table in the teaching journal.

pts: Score grammatical, sociolinguistic, discourse and strategic competence as separate, weighted bands, following Unit 27's model directly.
This gives specific, actionable feedback rather than a single vague overall impression score.
Weight the bands according to the task's actual communicative demands, not a fixed formula applied to every task type.

v: A speaking or writing task; chart paper

items: Choose a task learners will soon perform, for example a two-minute role-play at a railway enquiry counter.
Write one band for each component: grammatical, sociolinguistic, discourse and strategic.
For each band, write short descriptors at three or four levels.
Assign weights according to what the task demands most (see model language).
Trial it on two recordings or scripts first.
For younger learners, reduce to three levels and add pictures or symbols.
Support: start with two bands (grammar and one other) and add the rest over a term.
Challenge: learners use the rubric to score a model performance before their own task.

blocks.x: A four-band rubric for a railway-counter role-play (written for this book), with weights:

lines: Grammatical (25%): Uses question forms and times accurately enough that meaning is clear.
Sociolinguistic (30%): Uses polite requests (‘Could you tell me…?’) and suitable greetings and thanks.
Discourse (20%): Opens, sequences and closes the exchange naturally.
Strategic (25%): Checks understanding, asks for repetition, rephrases when stuck.

blocks.x: A weighting is a teaching decision. A formal debate (Unit 39) might weight discourse more heavily.

body: Purpose: to show an analytic communicative rubric at a glance. Content: a four-row grid, each row a competence with a small icon (bracket, handshake, chain, life-buoy) and a bar showing its weight. Style: tidy table. Board version: a four-row table with weights in the margin.

items: Google Docs (free) for a reusable rubric template; Google Classroom (free for schools) can attach rubrics to assignments.

blocks.x: A rubric written once on chart paper and displayed during the task.

points.sub: Matching the tool to the task
pts: A task-specific rubric, built around the particular task's genre and goals, generally outperforms a generic one-size-fits-all rubric.
This connects to Unit 33's genre awareness — a presentation rubric and a negotiation rubric should look meaningfully different.
Generic rubrics are more efficient to build but score real performance less precisely.

v: Two contrasting tasks (e.g. a presentation and a negotiation)

items: Take the generic four-band rubric from point 2.
For a presentation task (Unit 40), rewrite each descriptor using the language of that genre.
For a negotiation role-play (Unit 38), do the same.
Test each rewritten rubric on two or three recorded or observed performances, and adjust any descriptor that does not separate the bands clearly.
Decide which of your regular tasks justify a task-specific rubric and which can use the generic one.
Build a bank of task-specific descriptors that colleagues can share and adapt.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: The discourse band for two tasks:

lines: Presentation: Signposts the structure (‘First… Next… To sum up…’); links points to the main message.
Negotiation: Responds to the other person’s offer before making a counter-offer; summarizes what has been agreed.
Presentation: Addresses the audience appropriately; keeps a consistent, semi-formal register.
Negotiation: Softens disagreement (‘I see your point, but…’); avoids sounding abrupt.

blocks.x: The two genres (Unit 33) succeed in different ways; a generic descriptor cannot capture both precisely.

body: Purpose: to show generic and task-specific rubrics side by side. Content: three rubric cards with the same four row labels: a generic card, a presentation card (lectern icon) and a negotiation card (handshake icon), with changed words highlighted. Style: parallel layout. Board version: two columns with the changed words underlined.

items: Google Drive (free) shared folder for a descriptor bank.

blocks.x: A descriptor bank in a file in the staff room.

pts: Speaking and writing assessment is especially vulnerable to Unit 21's reliability concerns, since scoring involves real judgement.
Rater training and calibration sessions, comparing scores against benchmark samples, measurably improve consistency.
Double-marking a sample of assessments periodically catches drift before it affects overall course grading.

v: Three or four recorded or written sample performances; the rubric

items: Each teacher scores the same three samples independently, using the rubric.
Reveal scores together and note where they differ by more than one level.
Discuss the differences, pointing to specific evidence in the performance.
Agree a ‘benchmark’ score for each sample and annotate why.
Each term, double-mark a small sample (for example, one in ten scripts) to check for drift.
In a school with one English teacher, calibrate with colleagues at a cluster resource centre or DIET meeting.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: A: I gave the discourse band a 2. She never really finished the story.
B: I gave it a 3. Listen to 1:10: ‘After that… so finally…’ She sequences clearly until the end.
A: True. So the problem is the ending, not the whole organization.
B: Shall we say 3, and note ‘ending weak’ in the benchmark?

blocks.x: Rater training and the use of benchmark samples are standard practice in speaking and writing assessment because judgements vary even among experienced raters (Weigle 2002; Luoma 2004).

body: Purpose: to show calibration as convergence. Content: four teachers’ scores for one sample shown as scattered dots on a scale before discussion, clustered after it. Style: simple infographic. Board version: two number lines with dots.

items: Google Sheets (free) to compare scores across raters and spot large differences.
Audacity (free, open source) or a phone’s voice recorder to save speaking samples.

blocks.x: Photocopied scripts and a paper score grid.

pts: Holistic scoring gives one overall impression score; analytic scoring gives separate scores per criterion.
Analytic scoring gives more diagnostic detail; holistic scoring is faster and sometimes more consistent for overall ranking purposes.
Choose based on purpose — diagnostic feedback favours analytic; efficient overall grading sometimes favours holistic.

v: Six learner scripts; a holistic scale and an analytic rubric

items: Score six scripts quickly with a single holistic scale (1–5).
Score the same scripts with the four-band analytic rubric.
Compare the time taken, the information given, and any learners ranked differently.
Decide which method suits each purpose: diagnosing needs, giving feedback, or reporting a term grade.
Use holistic scoring for a quick class overview, then analytic scoring only for learners near a boundary.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Holistic: 3 out of 5, a competent account with some errors.
Analytic: Grammatical 2, Sociolinguistic 4, Discourse 4, Strategic 3.

blocks.x: The holistic score is quicker. The analytic score tells the learner and the teacher exactly what to work on: grammar needs attention, while appropriacy and organization are strengths. For feedback, the analytic version is more useful; for a quick ranking at the end of a term, the holistic version may be enough (Weigle 2002).

body: Figure 46.5 A single number or a profile

Purpose: to contrast holistic and analytic scoring. Content: one large dial pointing at 3 beside four labelled smaller dials pointing at 2, 4, 4 and 3. Style: clear. Board version: one circle with a number beside four circles with numbers.

items: Microsoft Forms or Google Forms (free) quiz mode with rubric-style scales for recording scores.

blocks.x: A class list with four narrow columns for analytic scores.

pts: Tie rubric bands to concrete CEFR can-do descriptors, connecting formal assessment back to Unit 2's placement framework.
This grounds abstract-sounding score bands in observable, specific behaviour, improving both validity and learner understanding.
It also creates continuity between placement, ongoing self-assessment (Unit 42), and formal performance assessment.

v: CEFR Companion Volume descriptors for one skill; the rubric

items: Choose one rubric band, for example strategic competence in speaking.
Find the relevant CEFR can-do descriptors at the levels you teach (Council of Europe 2020).
Rewrite them in plain language for your learners.
Use them as rubric descriptors and in learners’ self-assessment checklists (Unit 42).
For younger learners, use a simplified can-do scale with ‘I can…’ and a picture.
Support: fewer levels, each with one example.
Challenge: learners find evidence in their own recordings for each can-do statement.

blocks.x: Rubric levels for strategic competence, written for this book in the spirit of the CEFR:

lines: Level 1: I can ask someone to repeat or speak more slowly.
Level 2: I can check that someone has understood me, and say it another way if not.
Level 3: I can explain a word I don’t know by describing it (‘It’s a thing you use to…’).
Level 4: I can keep a conversation going when I don’t know a word, without long pauses.

blocks.x: A score of ‘3’ now has a meaning that the learner can see in their own performance. Placement (Unit 2), self-assessment (Unit 42) and formal assessment use the same language.

body: Purpose: to link rubric levels with observable behaviour. Content: a four-rung ladder, each rung a level with an ‘I can…’ statement; a learner stands on the third. Style: friendly. Board version: four lines of a ladder with short labels.

items: Council of Europe CEFR website (free) for official descriptors and the Companion Volume.
Canva for Education (free for teachers) for a printable can-do ladder.

blocks.x: A handwritten can-do ladder glued inside each notebook.

pts: Sharing, or even co-constructing, rubrics with learners builds understanding of what communicative competence actually involves.
This connects to Unit 43's peer-feedback principle — understanding criteria deeply is itself a learning process.
Transparent rubrics reduce the sense that assessment is an opaque, arbitrary judgement handed down from above.

v: Two contrasting model performances (recorded or written); chart paper

items: Show two model performances of the same task, one strong and one weaker (written or recorded for this purpose).
In groups, learners list what makes the strong one better.
Collect ideas and sort them under the four competence headings.
Together, write short descriptors for ‘excellent’, ‘good’ and ‘not yet’.
Learners use the class rubric to give peer feedback on a practice performance (Unit 43).
Learners brainstorm first in their home language, then work with the teacher to express criteria in English.
Support: provide criteria cards for learners to sort rather than generate.
Challenge: learners argue for the weighting of each band.

blocks.x: Learners’ first ideas, and how the teacher reshapes them:

lines: S1: The first one is better because he is not stopping.
T: Good. So one criterion is fluency, keeping going. Which heading does that belong to?
S2: The second girl says ‘Give me ticket’. It sounds rude.
T: Yes, that’s about being polite and suitable. Let’s put it under ‘appropriate language’.
Class descriptor, excellent: Speaks politely, keeps going, and fixes problems when the other person doesn’t understand.

blocks.x: Learners who understand the criteria can use them to evaluate and improve their own work, which is itself learning (Black and Wiliam 1998).

body: Purpose: to show co-construction. Content: a chart-paper rubric in learners’ handwriting, with sticky notes under each heading. Style: warm, handmade. Board version: four headings with ideas listed under each.

items: Padlet (free plan, limited number of boards) for collecting criteria ideas; Mentimeter (free plan) for a vote on weighting.

blocks.x: Sticky notes or slips of paper stuck under headings on the board.

body: Keep the language of the class rubric as close as possible to the language learners used. A descriptor they wrote themselves is easier to remember and apply than a polished one that you wrote for them.

pts: Patterns across a class's rubric scores should inform the next unit's language-focus priorities, not just individual grades.
This connects directly to Unit 9's reflective-practice principle, applied at the level of formal assessment data.
Assessment that doesn't feed back into planning has only completed half of its actual purpose.

v: Analytic scores for one class on one task

items: Enter the analytic scores for the whole class in a simple table.
Calculate the class average for each band.
Identify the weakest band for the class as a whole.
Plan the next unit’s language-focus stage (Unit 28) around the pattern, and note the change in your scheme of work.
After the next task, compare the band averages.
Share a simplified class profile with learners and ask what they want to work on next.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Class 9C, market role-play, average scores out of 4 (a fictional class):

lines: Grammatical 2.9 · Sociolinguistic 2.1 · Discourse 3.0 · Strategic 2.4

blocks.x: Decision: the class is weakest at appropriacy. Next unit’s language focus: polite requests and softening (Could I…? Would you mind…? I’m afraid…), practised through a repeated role-play. This is reflective practice (Unit 9) applied to assessment data: the rubric becomes a planning tool as well as a grading tool.

body: Purpose: to show assessment feeding planning. Content: a cycle of ‘Task’, ‘Score with rubric’, ‘Read the class profile’ and ‘Plan the next focus’, with a small bar chart of band averages at the centre. Style: clear. Board version: a circle with four labels.

items: Google Sheets or Microsoft Excel (free online version) with a simple average formula and bar chart.

blocks.x: Tally the scores on paper and draw a bar chart on the board.

body: For your next speaking task, score one class with a four-band rubric. Calculate the band averages and plan one ten-minute language-focus activity on the weakest band. Score the next task the same way and see whether that band moves.

dek: Unit 46 of 100: rubrics that actually score sociolinguistic, discourse and strategic competence, not just grammar dressed up as a communicative task.

aims.x: This unit asks whether the way we score speaking and writing matches the way we teach them. If the rubric at the end of a communicative task counts only grammar mistakes, learners will conclude that grammar is all that matters. The unit shows how to design, share and use rubrics that score the whole of communicative competence.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain why a grammar-only rubric is a validity problem for a communicative course;
build an analytic rubric with separate bands for grammatical, sociolinguistic, discourse and strategic competence;
weight rubric bands to suit the demands of a particular task;
decide when a task-specific rubric is worth the extra effort of building it;
improve rater reliability through calibration and double-marking;
choose between holistic and analytic scoring for a given purpose;
write band descriptors grounded in CEFR-style can-do statements;
involve learners in understanding and co-constructing criteria, and use class results to plan the next unit.

why: Why this matters. Tier II's methodology aims at the full model of communicative competence (Unit 27). Assessment that only scores grammar quietly contradicts everything else this tier teaches.

background.x: Assessment has a way of revealing what a course really values. A teacher may spend a fortnight on polite requests, turn-taking and repair in a bus-ticket role-play, then mark the performance by counting tense errors. The learners notice. This influence of testing on teaching and learning is called washback (Alderson and Wall 1993), and Unit 57 returns to it in depth.

The model of communicative competence introduced in Unit 27 gives us the categories we need. Michael Canale and Merrill Swain (1980) distinguished grammatical competence from sociolinguistic competence (using language appropriately to the situation), discourse competence (connecting sentences into coherent, cohesive talk or text) and strategic competence (managing breakdowns and gaps). Lyle Bachman (1990) later developed a fuller model for testing. A rubric that scores only one component has, in the terms of Unit 21, a validity problem: it does not measure what it claims to measure.

Performance assessment also brings a reliability problem. When a teacher listens to a two-minute talk and gives it a score, judgement is involved, and judgements differ between raters and drift over time. Clear descriptors, benchmark samples and rater training reduce this variation, though they never remove it (Weigle 2002; Luoma 2004), and a review of rubric research found that rubrics shared with learners can support both consistency and learning (Jonsson and Svingby 2007).

NEP 2020 calls for a shift from summative, rote-based assessment towards regular, formative and competency-based assessment, and proposes a holistic progress card that records more than marks (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020). NCF 2023 likewise stresses assessing competencies rather than recall (NCERT 2023). For English teachers, this means assessing what learners can do with the language, and recognizing that a learner who switches briefly into Kannada or Hindi to find a word, and then carries on in English, may be showing strategic competence, not failure.

items: Rubric audit. A short written audit of one existing marking scheme, showing marks by competence and one proposed change.
Calibration record. Annotated benchmark samples agreed with colleagues, with evidence of reduced differences between raters.
Task-specific rubric. A rubric for one genre, with weighting explained by the task’s demands.
Planning link. A class profile from rubric scores and the next unit’s language focus that responds to it.
What do your current marking schemes reward most? Is that what you most want learners to learn?
When did you last compare your scores with a colleague’s? What surprised you?
Which of your regular tasks deserve their own rubric?
How do learners find out what a good performance looks like in your class?
How do you treat a learner’s brief use of the home language during a speaking task?
What changed in your teaching the last time you looked at a whole class’s results?

terms.def: A method of marking in which separate scores are given for different criteria, such as content, organization, vocabulary and grammar, giving more diagnostic information than a single overall (holistic) score.
A statement describing the performance expected at one level of a rating scale, such as ‘Band 4: ideas are clearly organized with some linking errors’, used to guide consistent marking.
A piece of learner work agreed by raters to illustrate a particular band or level, used in training and calibration to help teachers mark consistently.
A process in which raters mark the same samples, compare their scores and discuss differences until they apply a rating scale consistently.
A description of what a learner can do in a language, as in the CEFR, used for setting goals, self-assessment and describing levels; for example, ‘I can write a short email inviting a friend.’
Assessing a performance as a whole and giving a single overall score or band, rather than separate scores for criteria such as content, organization and accuracy.
The consistency of scores given by different raters, or by the same rater at different times, to the same performance; it is improved by calibration and double-marking.

A scoring guide that sets out the criteria for assessing a piece of work and describes performance at each level. Shared in advance, a rubric makes expectations clear and supports self-assessment and peer assessment.

The effect of a test on teaching and learning, which may be positive or negative (Alderson and Wall 1993). Board examinations that test only reading and writing often lead to neglect of listening and speaking.
The relative importance given to different criteria or sections of an assessment, expressed in marks or percentages. A weighting is a teaching decision that signals what matters most.
